clue.text: Salad of two eggs, thistle? Lose it

indicators.note: a salad is a jumble of mixed ingredients tossed together, so the letters are tossed into a new order

blocks.note: two copies of the word egg
taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd recipe: a salad of two eggs and a thistle, which is enough to make anyone lose their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two eggs' must be read literally as the word written twice, giving the four Gs the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose it can mean losing control of yourself, and helpless laughter is one such collapse of composure.

clue.text: The French defending one supporting mob – there's some nerve!

indicators.note: to defend something is to stand around it, so one piece wraps another
in a down clue, a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes after in the answer

blocks.note: a mob is a gang
la is the feminine form of 'the' in French
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on the cheek of a French group backing up a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, the supporting piece is the lower one. 'There's some nerve!' looks like an exclamation about cheek, but it is the definition read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganglia are clusters of nerve cells, so in a plural sense they really are some nerve tissue.

clue.text: Primarily, Thomas Edison's science-advancing, long-standing arch-rival!

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letters of the following words count

blocks.note: the initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A tribute to the inventor who sparred with Thomas Edison for years while pushing science forward.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the name, and the same words describe the man. Nikola Tesla championed alternating current against Edison's direct current.
explanation.definitionFit: Nikola Tesla's rivalry with Edison during the 'war of the currents' is famous in the history of electrical engineering.

clue.text: Sourced in Kandahar is salty, spicy paste

indicators.note: something sourced in a place comes from within it, so the letters lie inside the run of words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the city name and into the next two words

explanation.surface: A food note: a salty, spicy paste obtained from Kandahar in Afghanistan.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles Kandahar, is and salty.
explanation.definitionFit: Harissa is a North African chilli paste flavoured with garlic and spices, used as a condiment and marinade.

clue.text: Infantrymen guided arrangers in orchestration

indicators.note: orchestrating music means arranging its parts anew, so the letters are scored in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers steered the musical arrangers while a piece was being orchestrated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guided' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grenadier Guards are a senior infantry regiment of the British Army, famous for ceremonial duty at Buckingham Palace.

clue.text: Good to roam freely, reaching farmhouse

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
to range is to wander widely

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys wandering freely until they come upon a farmhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: G as good appears on report cards and pencil grades.
explanation.definitionFit: A grange is a country house with farm buildings attached, historically an outlying farm belonging to a monastery.

clue.text: LA: it's in America, on the Gulf of Mexico

definitions.text: it's in America, on the Gulf of Mexico

blocks.note: first meaning: the postal abbreviation of a US state

blocks.clueFragment: it's in America, on the Gulf of Mexico
blocks.note: second meaning: a southern state with a coastline on that gulf

explanation.walkthrough: LA looks like Los Angeles, which is in America but on the Pacific; the Gulf of Mexico rules that out and points to the state with the same abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The state's official two-letter postal code is LA, and its southern coast borders the Gulf around New Orleans.

clue.text: Mandarin tests Ms. Thurman

blocks.note: SATs are standardised school tests in the UK and US
the actress Uma Thurman

explanation.surface: Someone who speaks Mandarin Chinese is examining the actress Uma Thurman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mandarin' looks like the language or an official, but here it is the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a variety of mandarin orange, a small loose-skinned citrus fruit originally from Japan.

clue.text: Burden hanging over setter and solver

blocks.note: a thing on another hangs over it
the setter and the solver together are 'us'

explanation.surface: A weight looms over both the puzzle's compiler and the person tackling it.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves as me and to the solver as you; together they are us.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a duty or responsibility laid on someone, the burden of having to do something.

clue.text: Once more assess, leave a true slamming

indicators.note: slamming something knocks it about violently, so its letters are battered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A reviewer is told to look again rather than leave a true slamming of the work in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slamming' reads as a harsh review, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To reevaluate is to judge or appraise something a second time, so 'once more assess' is a direct paraphrase.

clue.text: Scrapes together half of single answer

indicators.note: half of a word means only one of its two equal portions is kept

blocks.note: the back three of the six letters
ANS is a common abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Someone cobbles together just half of a single reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half of the word is taken, not the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To glean is to gather bit by bit from scattered sources, as gleaners once collected leftover grain after harvest.

clue.text: Gold ... bunch of wind ... American statesman

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a gust is a sudden burst of wind
US is short for the United States, hence American

explanation.surface: A dotted list sketches a US politician: gold, plenty of hot air, and an American statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American statesman' looks like one unit, but 'American' belongs to the wordplay; the statesman is Roman, not American.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus, first emperor of Rome, was a political leader and administrator, so he counts as a statesman.

clue.text: Essential to Health: roly-poly pudding's #4, after t'ai chi regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter, skipping one each time
a number sign with four points to the letter in fourth place
coming after means the following piece is placed behind the one it follows

blocks.note: roly-poly means plump, and fatty is an informal word for a plump person
the second, fourth and sixth letters
the fourth letter of the word

explanation.surface: A wellbeing magazine column claims roly-poly pudding and t'ai chi are essential to your health.
explanation.walkthrough: Health is italicised as if a magazine title. Roly-poly pudding is a British suet pudding rolled with jam; here 'roly-poly' is plump. The pudding's fourth letter follows the t'ai chi letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Certain fatty acids, such as omega-3, cannot be made by the body and must come from diet, so they are essential nutrients.

clue.text: Retaliation: what makes 'hit a toff' click!?

blocks.note: first meaning: paying back like with like
second meaning: playfully, the motive that makes striking a posh person make sense, getting even with the upper classes

explanation.walkthrough: A toff is a British word for an upper-class person. The second half is a whimsical cryptic description rather than strict wordplay: hitting a toff only clicks as payback.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means repaying an injury with an equivalent one, the very idea of a measured retaliation.

clue.text: Withdrawn, partly open Indian prince

indicators.note: something withdrawn is pulled back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a door that is ajar is slightly open

explanation.surface: A shy, reserved Indian prince who is only half open with people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawn' reads as a personality trait of the prince, and 'partly open' as reticence, but both are wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A raja is an Indian king or prince, the title used for rulers of the old princely states.

clue.text: US duffer plays green shot loudly

indicators.note: said loudly means spoken out, so what counts is the sound of the word

blocks.note: to putt is to play a gentle shot on a golf green

explanation.surface: An American golfing novice taps the ball on the green with a noisy stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duffer' and 'green' paint golf, which hides that the duffer is the definition, an American slang word for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Putz is American slang, from Yiddish, for a stupid or contemptible person, matching the British word duffer for an incompetent.

clue.text: Prince topless, tea to get more drawn out

definitions.note: a phrase for the verb meaning to make something last longer

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter is removed

blocks.note: Pr is an abbreviation for prince
oolong is a Chinese tea

explanation.surface: A prince with his shirt off is offered tea so that the afternoon drags on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' sits beside 'Prince' but acts on the tea: OOLONG loses its first O.
explanation.definitionFit: To prolong is to extend something in time, making a meeting or a visit longer than it would otherwise be.

clue.text: Announces cramps; oil massaged

indicators.note: a massage kneads and works the body over, so the letters are worked into new positions

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sports physio's notes: the patient reports cramps, so oil is rubbed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cramps' is a noun in the picture and part of the letters to be rearranged in the solving.
explanation.definitionFit: To proclaim is to declare something publicly and officially, which is what announcing means.

clue.text: A little manic, Ollie Reed portrays man seen with canary

indicators.note: a little of the phrase is a small part of it, so the letters sit inside

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the name

explanation.surface: The wild actor Oliver Reed, a touch manic, plays a man accompanied by a pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Reed was a British actor known for hellraising. The canary is the bird miners took underground to detect gas.
explanation.definitionFit: A collier is a coal miner, and miners once carried caged canaries to warn of poisonous gases in the pit.

clue.text: Arrived on a little isthmus in Med, took the plunge

indicators.note: just a little of the word is its opening letter
placed in means set inside the other piece
in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: arr. is the timetable abbreviation for arrives or arrived
the opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diver reaches a narrow strip of land in the Mediterranean and jumps into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took the plunge' looks like a dive off that isthmus, but it is the idiom for getting wed.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the plunge is an idiom for committing to something bold, most often a wedding.

clue.text: Actor, regularly loud, very very immodest and egotistical at the outset

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept
the outset is the start, so only opening letters are used

blocks.note: the first and third letters
V is the abbreviation for very
the same abbreviation again
the initials of the two adjectives

explanation.surface: A portrait of a thespian who is noisy, extremely vain and self-obsessed from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's adjectives describe the stereotype, so the surface is also a definition of the theatrical type. Luvvie is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Luvvie is British slang for an actor, especially a gushing, self-regarding one who calls everyone 'love'.

clue.text: Member of Steps, Beatle wife, 60s diva assembled somewhere in C Pacific

blocks.note: Ian 'H' Watkins was a singer in the British pop group Steps
Yoko Ono, John Lennon's wife
Lulu, the Scottish singer who rose to fame in the 1960s

explanation.surface: A fantasy pop line-up: a Steps singer, a Beatle's wife and a sixties star gather on a Pacific island.
explanation.walkthrough: Steps were a 1990s British pop group whose member went by the single letter H. 'C' stands for central.
explanation.definitionFit: Honolulu, capital of Hawaii, lies on Oahu in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, so it is a place in the central Pacific.

clue.text: Some 'hero' haltingly retiring  somewhere in Asia

indicators.note: some of the words means just a part of them is used
to retire is to go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A so-called hero, stammering and shy, withdraws to somewhere in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' reads as shy, but it is the instruction to turn the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: Lahore is a large city in Pakistan, capital of Punjab province, and so a place in Asia.

clue.text: Hearts of the vain yakuza captured in poetry

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: the centre letter
the middle pair
the middle pair

explanation.surface: The soul of a vain Japanese gangster is caught in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The yakuza are Japanese organised crime gangs, which fits a Japanese verse form.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiku is a Japanese verse form of three lines with five, seven and five syllables, so it is a kind of poetry.

clue.text: Everyman touring Ontario with Italian musician – and another

definitions.note: stands for another Italian musician, leaning on the words before it

indicators.note: a tour goes all round a region, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: the setter Everyman refers to himself as me
Ont. is the abbreviation for the Canadian province
the opera composer Giuseppe Verdi

explanation.surface: The setter goes on a tour of Canada accompanied by two Italian composers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian musician' looks like the definition, but it is wordplay for the opera composer; the definition is 'another', meaning a second Italian musician. Claudio Monteverdi was an early Baroque composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudio Monteverdi was a composer from Cremona, a pioneer of opera with L'Orfeo, so he is a further musician from Italy.

clue.text: Perhaps Murdoch's one seen in the Eye?

definitions.note: a thing seen in the eye; the definition is a phrase describing a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the first name of the novelist Murdoch
second meaning: the coloured ring of the eye

explanation.walkthrough: Murdoch and the italicised Eye suggest Rupert Murdoch and Private Eye, the British satirical magazine; but the Murdoch is the novelist Iris, and the eye is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch was a British novelist and philosopher, and the iris is the coloured muscular ring around the pupil.

clue.text: Makes progress with clue for 'the rags'?

blocks.note: first meaning: advances steadily, gains on someone
second meaning: read as a cryptic clue, its first word with 'ground' as a crushing signal would rearrange into 'the rags'

explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer itself works as wordplay, with its second word telling you to grind up its first and so produce the rags.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather ground is an idiom like gaining ground: moving forward or advancing on a rival in a race or contest.
